input.title: Reducer-level RBAC gates operations on action.context.signer.user.address so access control replicates with the document

input.description: Roles live in document state and every operation reads the signer address, throwing a typed error when unauthorized. Rejections surface as operation.error, not as thrown exceptions to callers.

input.content:
The `role-based-auth` recipe puts authorization **inside the reducer**, reading the signer off the action context. Because roles are ordinary document state, they replicate with the document — every peer enforces the same rules without a central policy service, and the rules hold no matter which editor, subgraph, or script fired the action.

The state is just address lists:

```graphql
type RoleBasedAuthState {
  creator: String
  admins: [String!]!
  members: [String!]!
  notes: [Note!]!
}
```

Every operation opens with the same guard, and role-mutating operations add `requireAdmin(state, address)`:

```ts
const address = action.context?.signer?.user?.address;
if (!address) throw new NotAuthorized("User is not authenticated");
```

The permission model is small and worth copying: `bootstrap` may be called by anyone but only once, and it makes the caller the permanent `creator` and first admin — creator auto-promotion, with no demotion path (`revokeAdmin` throws `CannotRevokeCreator`). It also throws `LastAdmin` rather than allowing the admin set to be emptied, so the document cannot be locked out. The domain action `writeNote` is gated on member-or-higher and throws `NotAuthorized` for a caller with no role.

**How rejection surfaces is the part that trips people up.** A thrown reducer error does not propagate to the caller as an exception. The framework captures it and records it as `operation.error` on the resulting document — the operation is still appended, and the state is unchanged. Callers detect rejection by inspecting the operation log, and tests must read `operations.global[n].error` rather than using `.toThrow()`.

Errors are a typed taxonomy generated into `gen/access/error.ts` (`AlreadyBootstrapped`, `CannotRevokeCreator`, `LastAdmin`, `AddressAlreadyAdmin`, `NotAuthorized`), so each failure is distinguishable rather than one generic denial.

Note the scope of the guarantee: this gates *writes* deterministically on every replica, but it does not hide state — anyone who can read the document reads the whole document, roles included.

Provenance: academy `05-Lookup/00-Cookbook.md`, Role-Based Auth recipe, academy 6.2.2-dev.45.

## Contradicts: policy in the auth scope (v6.2.2-dev.74)
The vault also holds the opposite mechanism: since v6.2.2-dev.74 the reactor can decide the same question from a **policy stored in the document's `auth` scope**, enforced at admission, replay and read, with no access check in any reducer. Both designs replicate with the document and both are supported — the Cookbook ships them as deliberate counterparts (`role-based-auth` here, `document-acl` there), "same outcome, opposite mechanism".

The boundary is where the rule lives, and it decides three things. **Reducer RBAC** bakes the rule into the model: it needs no feature flags, works on every reactor today, and can express anything code can — but changing the rule means shipping a new model version, and the check runs *inside* the reducer, so a refused write is still a stored operation carrying an error. **The auth scope** makes the rule data: inspectable, replicated, changeable at runtime, and refused *at admission* so nothing is stored — but it is staged behind feature flags, bounded by the version-1 grant and condition caps, and enforces nothing on a document whose policy was never initialized. Choose reducer RBAC for invariants that are part of what the model *is*; choose the auth scope for access that operators need to change without a release.
